<b>Siglo I</b>Plinio el Viejo describe e: 1st centuryPliny the Elder describes in his Natural History the lights that settle on masts during storms. Greek sailors called them Castor and Pollux: two lights were a good sign and a single one, a bad one.
<b>Edad Media</b>Toman el nombre de San: Middle AgesThey take their name from Saint Erasmus of Formia (St. Elmo), patron saint of sailors: seeing the glow was understood as his protection in the middle of a storm.
<b>1520</b>Antonio Pigafetta, cronista d: 1520Antonio Pigafetta, chronicler of the Magellan–Elcano voyage around the world, describes how St. Elmo's fire appeared at the top of the masts and reassured the crew.
<b>1750</b>Benjamin Franklin propone que: 1750Benjamin Franklin proposes that lightning is an electric spark and that a metal point discharges the clouds slowly and silently, with a glow like this one. This is where the lightning rod comes from.
El modelo del paso 3 es un problema de e: The model in step 3 is a problem of conducting spheres: two spheres joined by a wire are at the same potential, so the charge is shared in proportion to their radius and the field next to the surface is greater on the small one.
Se abre con dos esferas conductoras en e: It opens with two conducting spheres in SI: the hull, of 1 m and 5.56 µC (about 50 kV), and the tip, of 1 cm and at 20 m, with its charge as the unknown and the condition that both have the same potential. We get a charge of about 5.3·10<sup>−8</sup> C on the tip, 50 kV/m next to the hull and 4.75 MV/m next to the tip, above the 3 MV/m of air. It is slightly less than the 5 MV/m of the model because, at 20 m, the hull also raises the potential of the tip.

de campo entre la base de la nube y el m: of field between the base of the cloud and the sea.
La base de una nube de tormenta se carga: The base of a thundercloud becomes negatively charged and the sea, which conducts well, is left with positive charge just below. Between the two a vertical electric field appears, $E⃗$, pointing from the sea to the cloud.\n\nIn fine weather that field is about 100 V/m; under a storm it reaches 10 or 20 kV/m, a hundred times more.
El mástil se carga por inducción: The mast is charged by induction
entre la punta del mástil y el aire que: between the tip of the mast and the air around it.
El casco, los mástiles y el mar forman u: The hull, the masts and the sea form a single conductor. The negative cloud drives the electrons away towards the sea and leaves positive charge at the top, at the tips of the masts.\n\nIn equilibrium the whole conductor is at the same potential. If the tips are 5 m above the sea in a field of 10 kV/m, they are about $ΔV ≈ E h = 50 "kV"$ from the air around them.
Las cargas se amontonan en la punta: Charges pile up at the tip
La punta tiene 100 veces más carga por u: The tip has 100 times more charge per unit area than the hull.
Un modelo sencillo: dos esferas conducto:
A simple model: two conducting spheres joined by a wire, a large one (the hull, $R_1 = 1 "m"$) and a small one (the tip, $R_2 = 1 "cm"$). Being joined they have the same potential:

$V = Q_1/(4πε_0 R_1) = Q_2/(4πε_0 R_2)$

The small one takes less charge, but on a much smaller surface, so its charge density is greater: $σ_2/σ_1 = R_1/R_2 = 100$.
El campo en la punta es enorme: The field at the tip is enormous
El campo junto a la punta supera la rigi: The field next to the tip exceeds the dielectric strength of air.
Junto a un conductor el campo es $E = σ/: Next to a conductor the field is $E = σ/ε_0$, which for a sphere is $E = V/R$. With the same 50 kV, at the hull $E = (50 "kV")/(1 "m") = 50 "kV/m"$ and at the tip $E = (50 "kV")/(0.01 "m") = 5 "MV/m"$.\n\nDry air stops insulating at around 3 MV/m: that is its dielectric strength. At the tip it is exceeded; at the hull, not by a long way.
El aire se rompe: descarga corona: The air breaks down: corona discharge
Cada electrón arranca otro al chocar con: Each electron knocks another one loose when it collides with a molecule: they multiply.
En el aire siempre hay algún electrón li: In the air there is always some free electron, knocked loose by cosmic rays or natural radioactivity. In such an intense field, between collisions it gains enough energy to knock another electron out of a nitrogen or oxygen molecule, and those two knock out two more: it is an avalanche.\n\nBut the field falls quickly away from the tip (as $1/r^2$), so the avalanche stays in a layer a few millimetres thick around it: it is a corona discharge, not lightning.
La luz azul del Fuego de San Telmo: The blue light of St. Elmo's fire
Es la luz de las moléculas de nitrógeno: It is the light of excited nitrogen molecules: a cold plasma that does not burn.
Las moléculas de nitrógeno que la avalan:
The nitrogen molecules excited by the avalanche emit, on returning to their normal state, blue and violet light (and some ultraviolet). That is why the tips glow with a bluish shimmer and a crackling is heard.

It is a cold plasma with currents of microamperes: it burns or breaks nothing. Sailors took it as the protection of Saint Erasmus, St. Elmo. Today it is seen on aircraft wings, and the lightning rod uses the same idea: a point connected to ground that concentrates the field.

Try it yourself: with the slider you change the radius of the tip. Above about 1.7 cm the field, $E = V/R$, no longer reaches 3 MV/m and the glow goes out.
